analysis.title: "Supply Shocks Are Back": Goldman Says The 60/40 Needs A Third Leg, And It Isn't Crypto
key_insights: Goldman's commodities team (Daan Struyven) reports the BCOM commodities basket at +36% total return year-to-date, against +13% for the S&P 500, -5% for 10Y Treasuries and -8% for the 30Y. BCOM Energy is +98% and oil products +136%.
The classic 60/40 equity-bond portfolio is up 8% YTD with a 1.2 Sharpe, versus 65% for a Semi-Energy barbell (per a zerohedge post dated October 9, 2026).
Goldman recommends a positive commodities allocation, both tactically and structurally, even though its base case has crude and European gas prices moderating as Mideast supply adapts.

Since the Iran war began, equities and bonds have become unusually sensitive to energy prices. Over the past six months the daily correlation of Brent with the S&P 500 averaged nearly -0.5, and with 10Y yield changes nearly +0.6.

Goldman attributes the sensitivity to the size and uncertainty of the supply shock, resilient global GDP growth and five years of above-target inflation, which have led central banks to respond strongly to higher energy prices.

Goldman says that without the energy price rise since the war began, yields would likely have risen less and equities would likely have risen more, since strong earnings growth has outweighed multiple compression.

Goldman's base case is Brent at $90/bbl by end-2026. In a scenario where 2027 Gulf output stays 5mb/d below February levels, Brent reaches $140 in early 2027 and averages around $125 next year. Reported attacks on shipping in Hormuz have picked up in October.

Goldman lists the 2022 Russian gas shock, last year's Chinese rare earths shock and this year's Hormuz cross-commodity shock as evidence that commodity disruption risk has risen structurally, driven by supply concentration, US-China competition in AI and geopolitics, and geopolitical fragmentation.
Supply concentration: DR Congo produces roughly 70% of cobalt, and China does about 90% of rare earth refining and roughly 70% of lithium refining.

Demand shocks dominated in the 2000s and 2010s and moved stocks and yields in the same direction, which made bonds a hedge. Supply shocks have been more prominent over the past five to six years and move stocks and yields in opposite directions.
The 60-month rolling correlation between S&P returns and 10Y yield changes was positive for two decades, fell after Russia-Ukraine and now sits around -0.5, back to pre-2000 levels.

Goldman's asset allocation team finds regime-neutral optimal allocations to commodities are likely higher once a longer history of supply-driven price shocks is included. The hit ratio can be low, but the hedge pays with convexity.

Last week the oil/rates/equities correlations broke down as AI credit concerns took over, per Goldman's EU index vol desk (Jonathan Luey): hyperscaler CDS widened 14bp, data-center CDS 69bp, the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.5%, semis fell 11.8%, and 10Y yields fell 17bp while Brent rose almost 5% on Houthi missiles and sunken tankers.
Goldman estimates a $25 risk premium is already in front-month Brent, so it prefers hedges with more asymmetric upside and attractive valuations over spot energy.
Goldman recommends long European summer 2027 gasoline (EBOB Jun27) futures and TTF 2027Q1 call spreads for European gas.
On the structural side Goldman favors copper, gold and select power markets such as PJM, where data center demand is running into supply limits. A separate post on these is due.

tension_points.bull_case: Bonds still hedge equities when scares are about growth, as last week's 17bp drop in 10Y yields during a 5.5% Nasdaq 100 fall showed.
tension_points.bear_case: Supply shocks move stocks and yields in opposite directions, so the 60/40 does not hedge. The 60-month rolling correlation is around -0.5 and this year's scares come from Hormuz.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Central banks regaining the ability to look through an oil spike would restore the old hedge.
